title.text: Hey, welcome back to The Life of a Query.
This one is the connection: everything that happens before your SQL even arrives.
Three things. How a session gets built, what the handshake actually sends, and why MySQL and PostgreSQL disagree about what a connection even is.
Let's get into it.

handshake.text: Nothing runs until a session exists.
It announces its version, and the authentication methods it will accept.
The client answers with credentials. Only then does a session exist.
And here is the part that actually matters.
Building a connection is expensive. Keeping one open is cheap.
That asymmetry is the entire argument for connection pooling.

engines.text: But a connection is not the same thing in both engines.
MySQL gives each connection a thread, inside one server process.
Threads share an address space, so a new connection is cheap.
But one bad thread can take the whole server down with it.
PostgreSQL forks a separate operating system process for every connection.
Processes are isolated. A crash costs you one backend, not the server.
But each one costs real memory. That is why PgBouncer exists.

end.text: So: the server speaks first, the client answers, and only then does a session exist.
MySQL gives you a thread. PostgreSQL gives you a process.
Either way, the connection is the expensive part. Pool it.
Next, we parse.

title.text: Welcome back.
Last time the client and the server agreed on who you are. Now the query itself arrives, as a string.
Three things. How that text becomes tokens, how tokens become a tree, and the extra stage PostgreSQL runs that MySQL does not.
Let's parse it.

tokens.text: To the server, your query arrives as a string. Nothing more.
The first job is lexing: cutting that string into tokens. Keywords, identifiers, literals, punctuation.
A typo fails here, before anything touches a table.

tree.text: Next, those tokens are assembled into a tree.
The root is the statement. Beneath it hang the target list, the from clause, and the where clause.
But this is still only syntax. The tree says the query is shaped correctly. It does not yet know whether the users table exists, or what type the id column is.

pipelines.text: Resolving those names is a separate stage, and here the two engines differ.
MySQL goes parser, resolver, optimizer. Three steps.
PostgreSQL goes parser, analyzer, rewriter, planner. Four.
That extra rewriter stage is what expands a view into the query that selects from it, and what makes PostgreSQL rules work at all.

end.text: Lexing, then parsing, turns text into a syntax tree, so a typo never reaches a table.
The parse tree is syntax only. Resolving names and types comes after.
And PostgreSQL adds a rewriter stage, which is how views and rules are expanded.
Next, we plan.

title.text: Welcome back.
Your query is a tree now. The server still has to decide how to answer it.
Three things. Why one query has many possible plans, how to read the one the server chose, and where its numbers actually come from.
Let's take a look.

candidates.text: One query. Several ways to answer it.
The server could scan every row in the table. It could build a bitmap of matching pages. Or it could walk the primary key index straight to the row.
The planner prices each one, in arbitrary cost units, and takes the cheapest.
Here that is the index scan, at eight point three, against eighteen hundred for the sequential scan.
Note what it did not do. The planner never asks which plan is fastest. It asks which plan it estimates is cheapest, and it is only as right as its statistics.

explain.text: You can see the estimate yourself. EXPLAIN shows the plan. EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually runs it.
The cost numbers are the guess, in planner units: startup cost, then total cost.
The actual time numbers are the measurement, in milliseconds.
When the actual row count is far from the estimate, your statistics are stale. That is a job for ANALYZE, not a bad planner.

statistics.text: So where do those numbers come from?
MySQL samples index pages at plan time, in what it calls index dives. Column histograms exist, but they are opt in.
PostgreSQL keeps histograms, most common values and null fractions in pg_statistic, and the autovacuum daemon re-runs ANALYZE as your tables drift.
Both of them search join orders: greedily in MySQL, and in PostgreSQL exhaustively for a few tables, then genetically past a threshold.

end.text: The planner prices every candidate and picks the cheapest estimate, not the fastest plan.
EXPLAIN gives you the estimate. EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs it and gives you the truth.
And a big gap between estimated and actual rows means stale statistics.
Next, we execute.

title.text: Welcome back.
The plan is chosen. Now something has to actually run it.
Three things. Why execution is a pull and not a push, what that means for LIMIT and ORDER BY, and why your reads never really touch the disk.
Let's run it.

pull.text: Here is the thing most people get backwards. Nobody runs the whole query.
Execution is a pull. Each node asks its child for one row, and rows travel back up one at a time.
This is why LIMIT is fast. The limit node stops asking after ten rows, so the scan below it never reads the rest of the table.
And it is why ORDER BY is not. A sort cannot return its first row until it has pulled every row from its child. That is a blocking node, and it is the one that spills to disk.

buffer.text: Underneath the scan, there is one more thing to understand. The scan does not read disk. It reads pages.
If the page it wants is already in the buffer pool, that is a hit, and it costs nanoseconds.
If it is not, that is a miss. The server reads from disk and evicts something to make room.
This is the only number that really matters. Tuning a database is mostly arranging for the pages you need to already be in memory.

memory.text: Both engines cache pages. They disagree about how.

InnoDB opens its files with O_DIRECT and owns the memory outright, so you give the buffer pool most of the machine. A split young and old list keeps one big scan from flushing everything that matters.

PostgreSQL shares with the kernel page cache, so a page can sit in both. The usual advice is about a quarter of RAM. It sweeps a usage counter in a ring instead of a strict least recently used list, and gives big sequential scans a small private ring so they cannot evict the whole cache.

end.text: Execution is a pull. Each node asks its child for one row, so LIMIT really does stop the scan.
Sort and hash nodes block. They must drain their child before returning anything.
And reads either hit the buffer pool or they hit disk. That difference is most of your latency.
Next, we return.

title.text: Welcome back. Last one.
The rows exist. Now they have to get back to you.
Three things. Why a result set is a stream and not a parcel, what each engine puts on the wire, and the default that quietly runs you out of memory.
Let's finish it.

streaming.text: The result set is not a parcel. It is a stream.
Rows leave the executor as they are found, not when the query ends. They are framed by the wire protocol, handed to your driver, and arrive in your code one at a time.
Which means a driver that materialises the whole result set before giving you the first row throws all of that away, and your memory with it.

protocol.text: The frames look much the same on both sides.
MySQL sends a column count, then a column definition per column, then one packet per row, then an OK packet to finish.
PostgreSQL sends a row description, then a data row per row, then command complete and ready for query.

Same shape. And here is the trap: the server streams, but your driver usually does not. That default is where out of memory on a big SELECT comes from. A cursor, or a driver fetch size, is what makes it incremental.

end.text: The server emits rows as it finds them. The result set is a stream.
Both wire protocols describe the columns once, then send rows, then signal completion.
And most drivers buffer everything by default. A cursor or a fetch size is what makes it incremental.
That is the life of a query, from connection to result.

title.text: Welcome back. Part two starts here.
You have seen how a query travels. Now we take the operations one at a time, starting with SELECT.
Three things. The order the clauses actually run in, why that order explains a classic error, and what SELECT star really costs.
Let's select.

order.text: SELECT is the first word you write, and almost the last thing that runs.
The server starts at FROM. It has to know which table before it can do anything else.
Then WHERE throws rows away, and GROUP BY and HAVING reduce what is left. Only then does SELECT choose the columns.
ORDER BY sorts the survivors, and LIMIT cuts the list short.
Which explains a classic error: you cannot use a column alias in WHERE, because when WHERE runs, the alias does not exist yet.

star.text: Which brings us to SELECT star.
Naming your columns is not about typing less. It is about how much the server has to read.
A wide row spread across several pages costs several page reads. Ask for two narrow columns and the index alone may answer you.
That is a covering index, and it is the difference between a millisecond and a hundred.

end.text: Clauses run FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY, LIMIT — not the order you type them.
That order is why an alias from SELECT cannot be used in WHERE.
And SELECT star is a read-volume decision, not a typing one.
Next, we insert.

title.text: Welcome back.
A row has to get onto disk, and survive a power cut on the way.
Three things. Why the write does not go to the table first, what the log actually guarantees, and how the two engines protect a half-written page.
Let's write one.

write.text: An INSERT does not go to the table. Not first.
The row is written into a page in memory, and the change is appended to the write-ahead log.
The log is flushed to disk. Only then does COMMIT return to you.
The page itself might be written minutes later. Or never, if it changes again first.
This is why a database survives a power cut. The log is the truth; the table catches up.

durability.text: Both engines work this way. They disagree about the dangerous part.
A page is bigger than a disk sector, so a crash can leave it half written. Neither engine can trust such a page.
MySQL writes every page twice: once into a doublewrite buffer, then into place. A torn page is recovered from the copy.
PostgreSQL instead writes the entire page into the log the first time it changes after a checkpoint.

end.text: The write-ahead log is flushed before COMMIT returns; the table page can wait.
That ordering is the whole of crash durability.
A torn page is the real danger, and each engine pays differently to survive it.
Next, we update.

title.text: Welcome back.
An UPDATE looks like it changes a row in place. It does not.
Three things. What actually happens to the old value, why two sessions can see different data at the same moment, and who clears up afterwards.
Let's change something.

mvcc.text: An UPDATE does not overwrite the row.
PostgreSQL writes a new version of it and marks the old one dead. The dead one stays in the table.
InnoDB writes the new value in place, and keeps the old value in the undo log.
Either way, a reader that started before your change still sees the old value. That is multi-version concurrency control.
It is also why a reader never blocks a writer, and a writer never blocks a reader.

cleanup.text: But somebody has to clear up.
In PostgreSQL that is autovacuum. It marks dead tuples reusable, so the table stops growing.
In InnoDB it is the purge thread, discarding undo records that no transaction can still see.
Block either one with a long-open transaction and you get bloat: in the table, or in the undo log.

end.text: Nothing is overwritten. The old value survives as a dead tuple or an undo record.
That is what lets readers and writers run without blocking each other.
And an idle transaction left open is what turns that into bloat.
Next, we delete.

title.text: Welcome back.
DELETE is the operation people most expect to free disk space. It does not.
Three things. What a delete actually writes, why the file stays the same size, and what you run when you genuinely need the space back.
Let's remove some rows.

mark.text: It marks the row dead, writes that change to the log, and returns.
The bytes are still sitting on the page until cleanup runs.
Which is why deleting a million rows gives you back no disk at all.

space.text: So how do you actually get the space?
VACUUM makes the dead space reusable, so new rows fill it instead of extending the file.
VACUUM FULL rewrites the whole table and does return the space — behind an exclusive lock nobody else can work through.
MySQL's equivalent is OPTIMIZE TABLE, which rebuilds the tablespace the same way.
And for an entire table, TRUNCATE is a different operation: it drops the data files instead of marking rows one by one.

end.text: DELETE marks rows dead and logs the change; the bytes stay until cleanup.
Ordinary vacuum makes space reusable, not returnable.
VACUUM FULL, OPTIMIZE TABLE or TRUNCATE are what actually shrink the file — and they all take heavy locks.
Next, we join.

title.text: Welcome back.
A join is the operation most likely to turn a fast query into a slow one.
Three things. The three strategies a planner can choose, what each one is good at, and how it decides between them.
Let's join two tables.

strategies.text: There are three ways to join two tables, and the planner picks one.
Nested loop: for every row on the left, look up the matches on the right. Excellent when the left side is tiny and the right side is indexed.
Hash join: build a hash table from the smaller side, then stream the larger side past it. Excellent for big unsorted joins, but it wants memory.
Merge join: sort both sides, then walk them in step. Cheap when they are already sorted, expensive when they are not.

choosing.text: It estimates how many rows each side will produce, and prices all three.
Get those estimates wrong and it picks a nested loop over a million rows, which is how a query goes from milliseconds to minutes.
MySQL used only nested loops until version eight point zero point eighteen. PostgreSQL has had all three for decades.

end.text: Nested loop, hash join, merge join — one query, three very different costs.
The planner prices them from its row estimates, so a bad estimate is a bad join.
A nested loop over a large unindexed side is the classic disaster.
Next, indexes.

title.text: Welcome back.
Everything we have said about fast lookups has assumed an index. Now we open one up.
Three things. What a B-tree lookup actually does, how the two engines store the rows at the bottom, and when an index makes things worse.
Let's look inside.

btree.text: An index is a tree, and a lookup is a walk down it.
Start at the root. Compare your value, pick a branch, repeat.
Three or four levels reaches any row in a table of millions, because every level multiplies the fan-out.
That is the whole trick: a handful of page reads instead of a scan of everything.

storage.text: The leaves are where the engines part company.
In InnoDB, the table is the primary key index. The row itself lives in the leaf.
So a secondary index stores the primary key, and reading a column it does not contain costs a second descent.
PostgreSQL keeps the table as an unordered heap, and every index points at a physical row location instead.
Which is why every index costs more writes, and why an index nobody reads is pure tax.

end.text: A lookup is three or four page reads down a tree, not a scan.
InnoDB puts the row in the leaf; PostgreSQL points at a heap location.
Every index you add is paid for on every write.
Next, transactions.

title.text: Welcome back. Last one.
Everything so far has been one operation. Transactions are how you make several of them behave as one.
Three things. What COMMIT and ROLLBACK actually do, the four isolation levels, and which one each engine gives you by default.
Let's finish the series.

lifecycle.text: BEGIN. Do the work. Then COMMIT, or ROLLBACK.
In between, nothing you have done is visible to anyone else.
COMMIT flushes the log and makes your work durable and visible at the same instant.
ROLLBACK throws it away: InnoDB walks the undo log backwards, while PostgreSQL simply never marks your new tuples live.
Which means in PostgreSQL a rollback is nearly free, and in InnoDB a huge one is not.

isolation.text: The interesting question is what you can see while somebody else is writing.
Read uncommitted lets you see their unfinished work. Almost nobody wants that.
Read committed gives every statement a fresh snapshot. This is PostgreSQL's default.
Repeatable read gives the whole transaction one snapshot. This is MySQL's default.
Serializable promises the result matches some serial order, and will abort you to keep that promise.

end.text: COMMIT makes work durable and visible at one instant; ROLLBACK discards it.
The four isolation levels trade visibility anomalies against concurrency.
PostgreSQL defaults to read committed, MySQL to repeatable read — the same code behaves differently on each.
That is the whole series: connection to commit.
